title: Did the Worst Business Advice in History Make This Man Rich?
description:
Timothy Dexter (1747-1806) of Newburyport, Massachusetts, is remembered as the man who shipped coal to Newcastle and bed warmers to the tropics, and got rich every time. How much of it really happened? Some of it is legend, some of it is his own bragging, and some of it is true.

Chapters
0:00 Bed warmers to the tropics?
0:28 A poor boy from Malden
0:58 Worthless money
1:31 The worst advice
2:17 In his own words
3:12 Lord Timothy
4:03 The fake funeral
4:39 A book with no stops
5:00 Fool or genius?

Facts used: Dexter was born in Malden, Massachusetts, on Jan. 22, 1747, left school at 8 for farm work and was apprenticed to a tanner at 16. He moved to Newburyport in 1769 and in 1770 married Elizabeth Frothingham, a widow with money; he sold hides, gloves and moose-hide breeches, and she ran a shop. After the Revolution he bought depreciated paper money; the federal government paid off the old Continental bills at about 1 percent of face value, while Massachusetts paid its own notes in full. The stories of rivals' bad advice, coal to Newcastle during a miners' strike, and mittens resold to Siberia come from later accounts (Samuel Knapp's Life of Lord Timothy Dexter and others) and are told here as legend. In his own book, A Pickle for the Knowing Ones (1802; about 8,800 words), Dexter wrote that he dreamed of warming pans three nights running, sent about 42,000 to the West Indies in nine vessels, that they were used for cooking and that he cleared 79 percent; that he shipped 21,000 Bibles to the West Indies in 21 vessels at about 100 percent profit; and that he bought 340 tons of whalebone. He bought a mansion on High Street, added minarets and a gilt eagle, called himself Lord Timothy Dexter, and had about 40 wooden statues carved by the ship carver Joseph Wilson, with Washington, Adams and Jefferson on the arch, plus Napoleon, William Pitt, Franklin and others, lions, and two statues of himself, one with the sign "I am the first in the East, the first in the West, and the greatest philosopher in the Western world." The fish seller Jonathan Plummer wrote verses in his praise. The mock funeral (about 3,000 people) and the caning of his wife come from the earliest accounts, written down years later; he called his wife "the gost" in his book. A later edition of the book added a page of punctuation marks. Dexter died in Newburyport in October 1806 at 59. The Great September Gale of 1815 toppled most of the statues, which were auctioned off or burned; the William Pitt statue is at the Museum of Old Newbury, and the house still stands on High Street as a private home. Knapp wrote that Dexter was no fool and that his ventures did not succeed by luck.

The scenes are an animated dramatization.
